title: Cross-Region Arbiter/Bridge Topology — Active/Assist Control Plane Sketch
summary: Sketch of a hybrid "active-assist" control plane topology: local active control planes per region paired with a lightweight cross-region arbiter/bridge to coordinate leases, routing policy decisions, and DR handoffs. Focus is on reduced tail-latency, controlled failover, and safe leader transitions without full global consensus dependencies.
body:
Context and motivation:

We need a middle-ground between: (A) fully active-active global control plane (fast local decisions but complex split-brain handling) and (B) strictly active-passive with global leader (simple safety but high failover latency and dependency on global consensus). Our product requires: low-latency routing decisions, tenant affinity guarantees, simple DR playbooks for enterprise SLAs, and the ability to operate with partial inter-region network failures.

Proposal (Active-Assist topology):

High level:
- Each region runs a full-featured local control plane instance responsible for serving routing policy queries, local rollouts, and per-tenant state that is region-scoped.
- A lightweight cross-region Arbiter/Bridge (a set of small stateless microservices with a compact durable store) provides global coordination for: lease arbitration (when a region must perform a global action), topology demarcation for routing policies (which region is authoritative for a tenant), and conflict-resolution hints.
- Local control planes operate as "active" by default for local decisions; for global writes (model pinning, global rollout toggles, tenant global config) they acquire a short lease mediated by the Arbiter.

Key components:
- Local Control Plane (LCP): handles per-region routing, local rollouts, metrics ingestion, and local KV for ephemeral state.
- Arbiter/Bridge Cluster: small replicated cluster (3 nodes per geo) exposed via a cross-region gossip or secure RPC. Responsible for short-term leases, lease history, and conflict markers. Not intended to be the source-of-truth for large config (those stay in primary config store).
- Lease Manager: lightweight API used by LCP to obtain preemptible leases for global actions (TTL-based, renew by heartbeat).
- Routing Policy Engine (RPE): runs in LCP but consults the Arbiter for tie-breakers when policies from multiple regions conflict (e.g., tenant moved).
- Demarcation log: compact append-only ledger in Arbiter for critical handoffs (tenant ownership transfers, emergency failover markers).

Routing policies and behavior:
- Default: latency-first with tenant affinity. LCP serves requests if healthy and below local SLOs.
- Cost-tiering: route to cheaper region if latency within configured budget. Policies can be per-tenant with priority lists.
- Write-affinity: writes for tenant metadata prefer the owner region; read-affinity can be served locally with last-known-good caches.
- Fallback tiers: (1) local LCP, (2) peer region with same continent, (3) remote region fallback. Arbiter can override for emergency consignment.

Leader election / arbitration model:
- Not full consensus for normal ops. Use lease-based arbitration with the Arbiter acting as a fast tie-breaker:
  - LCP tries to act alone for local decisions.
  - For any global write or demarcation change, LCP requests a short lease from Arbiter (e.g., 3s TTL, renew every 1s).
  - Arbiter grants at-most-one lease per tenant/namespace. Grants are recorded to ledger to provide post-facto auditability.
- Advantages: cheap path for common local ops; explicit and auditable handoffs for global ops.
- Degradation: if Arbiter unavailable, LCPs can use a conservative fallback: block global writes and enter a tentative mode where they may serve reads with an extra safetynet token in RPCs.

Failure modes and mitigation:
- Arbiter partition/outage:
  - Mitigation: LCPs continue local reads and local-only rollouts. Global writes are paused or queued. Operators can invoke an emergency manual lease via runbook.
- Split-brain between two regions starting global writes simultaneously:
  - Arbiter lease prevents this in normal conditions. If Arbiter was partitioned and both LCPs acted, detection relies on ledger reconciliation and automated repair tasks that detect conflicting demarcations and generate alerts + rollback proposals.
- Long network partitions with slow healing:
  - Prefer availability for reads, but require manual verification for global config changes older than N minutes.
- Arbiter compromised or Byzantine:
  - Arbiter kept minimal; don't store secrets there. Arbiter decisions are signed and stored; an offline reconciliation verifies signatures and a separate audit trail exists in primary config store.

DR and operational runbook (high level):
- Normal failure (single region outage):
  1) Reachability: route traffic to tier-2 regions (same continent) automatically using RPE with cached policies.
  2) If tenant owner region is down > 5m, Arbiter can assign temporary ownership to a recovery region via emergency lease (manual approval optional for enterprise customers).
  3) Post-failover: run reconciliation job to move durable tenant state back when owner region is healthy.
- Arbiter outage but most regions healthy:
  1) Pause global rollouts. Notify infra on-call.
  2) If outage > 15m, allow escalation path: a signed operator-issued manual lease drawn from audited keys.
- Full-control-plane catastrophe (platform-wide):
  1) Promote backup control plane (static DR region) via out-of-band process documented in DR runbook.
  2) Issue global rollback of recent demarcation changes if necessary.

Testing, validation, and metrics:
- Injected partition tests in staging that emulate: arbiter down, inter-region high-latency, split-brain writes.
- Contract tests for Lease Manager (TTL expiry, renew races) with deterministic clocks.
- SLOs to measure: lease-grant latency P50/P95, failed-lease rate, cross-region reconciliation lag, routing misroute rate, tenant-affinity violations.
- Logs: every lease grant/renew/revoke must have request id, region id, tenant id, and trace id.

Rollout strategy:
- Canary: enable Arbiter consults for 10% of tenants in a single region. Verify metrics and expedition paths.
- Gradual ramp: expand to multiple regions and then to 100% tenant coverage.
- Safety gates: no global writes allowed unless Arbiter P99 latency < 200ms for two consecutive hours.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Why not full active-active with CRDTs? CRDTs solve some conflict problems but introduce eventual convergence semantics that are hard for tenant-config and rollout correctness. They also complicate audits and enterprise compliance.
- Why not central global leader? Central leader reduces complexity but increases latency and a single point-of-failure for all global operations.
- Active-Assist balances: local low-latency common path + explicit, auditable global coordination for the uncommon global mutations.

Open questions / TODOs:
- TTL sizing: 3s TTL feels sensible but needs tuning per region-latency profiles. Run load tests to pick defaults.
- Arbiter placement: co-locate arbiter replicas in major regions (us-west/us-east/eu-west) or run a separate smaller fleet? Cost/latency tradeoffs.
- Operational keys and manual lease process: define signatory flow for enterprise emergency leases.
- Data model: how compact should the demarcation ledger be? Append-only with compaction vs. snapshotting.

Action items:
- Marcus: prototype Lease Manager API + minimal Arbiter client (2w spike).
- Jules: create staging partition test harness for arbiter outage (1w).
- Priya: draft operator-runbook and manual lease UI mockups (this doc -> runbook, 1w).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight and orthogonal to our primary config store (we don't replace it). Goal is to reduce blast radius and provide predictable, auditable handoffs for global operations without forcing every decision through an expensive global consensus loop.

References and links:
- existing multiregion notes (internal): see platform-engineering/region-fabric-decision-log for background on region fabrics.
- related PR: github.com/redwood/infra/pull/5678 (lease manager prototype).

Unresolved: formal proof obligations for no-split-brain under Arbiter quorum loss; we should sketch invariants and run a TLA+ or simplified model-checking pass if this design is selected for implementation.

End of sketch.
